content:
The objection says that a woman cannot lead men in prayer, that a mixed Friday prayer led by a woman in New York in 2005 was condemned, and that Islam therefore denies women religious authority.

This article aims to provide context to the objection, insha'Allah, in six points that separate two questions. One is who may lead a congregation in prayer.

The other is whether women hold religious authority at all. The record gives different answers to each.

Abu Dawud 591 and 592 report that the Prophet told Umm Waraqa to lead "the people of her house". The chain runs through al-Walid ibn Jumay' and two narrators whose standing is unknown, Layla bint Malik and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Khallad.

Al-Albani graded the report fair, and Shu'ayb al-Arna'ut graded it weak. Al-Daraqutni's version limits her to leading women.[1]

A'isha and Umm Salama led other women in prayer, standing in the middle of the row.[2]

Ibn Rushd reports that Abu Thawr and al-Tabari allowed a woman to lead without restriction. The same view is ascribed to al-Muzani. These views come to us as reports in later works, and the treatises that held them do not survive.[3]

A woman academic led a mixed Friday prayer in New York on 18 March 2005. Many prominent scholars condemned it, and some Muslims defended it.[4]

Mohammad Akram Nadwi's biographical dictionary of women scholars of hadith, al-Wafa' bi-Asma' al-Nisa', runs to 43 volumes and more than 10,000 entries. His al-Muhaddithat is the English version of its preface.[5]

Women narrated hadith, taught men and issued legal opinions. The rule on leading the prayer is a rule about one act of worship.[5]

1 Timothy 2:12 says: "I do not permit a woman to teach or to have authority over a man." 1 Corinthians 14:34 tells women to be silent in the churches.[6]

The Muslim rule concerns one role in one act of worship, while women taught, narrated and gave rulings to men and women alike.

The majority rule restricts one role in worship, and the record of women's learning answers the wider charge. Our related articles are 7 women in the Prophet's life who shaped Islam and 7 things to know before your first Friday prayer. Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Sunan Abi Dawud 591-592; Ibn Hajar, al-Isaba, under Umm Waraqa; the hadith texts are on searchtruth.com.
  2. 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Musannaf, no. 5086; al-Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra, the chapter on a woman leading women.
  3. Ibn Rushd, Bidayat al-Mujtahid, the book of prayer, on the imamate; al-Nawawi, al-Majmu', on the same question.
  4. Juliane Hammer, American Muslim Women, Religious Authority, and Activism: More Than a Prayer (Austin: University of Texas Press, 2012).
  5. Mohammad Akram Nadwi, al-Muhaddithat: The Women Scholars in Islam (Oxford: Interface, 2007).
  6. 1 Timothy 2:11-12; 1 Corinthians 14:34-35.
